clue.text: Welsh friend of German composer

definitions.meaning: in Welsh, ... is a term of endearment meaning dear or little one, used to a friend
Johann Sebastian, the Baroque master of Leipzig

explanation.surface: A Welsh companion of some German musician.
explanation.definitionFit: One word serves as a Welsh endearment for a pal and as the surname of the Leipzig cantor Johann Sebastian.

clue.text: Sky-high measurement found as, we hear, hospital admits one with upset stomach

indicators.note: signals that the little word 'as' is taken by its sound, spoken with a buzzing final letter

parts.note: the word as written, pronounced
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: upset means turned over, so the stomach word is read backwards in this down clue

parts.note: tum is an informal word for stomach
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A hospital takes in a patient with an upset stomach, somehow connected to an astronomical reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns TUM into MUT. 'admits' is only a joining word here: the H for hospital simply ends the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An azimuth is an angular bearing of a celestial body measured around the horizon, a reading taken of things high in the sky.

clue.text: Computer always one step ahead of IBM

definitions.text: Computer always one step ahead of IBM

parts.words: Computer always one step ahead of IBM
parts.note: each letter of the name of the computer in 2001: A Space Odyssey comes one place before the matching letter of IBM in the alphabet

explanation.surface: A rival machine keeps outpacing the big American computer firm.
explanation.walkthrough: Shift each of I, B, M back one letter of the alphabet and you get the name of Kubrick's murderous computer; it is 'ahead' in alphabetical order.
explanation.definitionFit: The rogue computer of the film 2001 has a name formed by stepping each letter of IBM one place earlier in the alphabet.

clue.text: Films promise to show you e.g. Bilbo's Sting

parts.note: shorts are brief films
to give your word is to promise

explanation.surface: Short movies vow to display the hobbit's famous blade.
explanation.definitionFit: Sting is the small elven blade Bilbo carries in The Hobbit, a short weapon by human standards.

clue.text: May 1923, comedy actor

parts.note: a comic performer born in May 1923, whose centenary fell around this puzzle's date

explanation.surface: A birth date and a profession, like an anniversary listing.
explanation.walkthrough: This is one of the puzzle's anniversary clues: Eric, the English comic actor and writer, was born on 4 May 1923.
explanation.definitionFit: The English comedian Eric of that surname, known for television sitcoms, was born in May 1923.

clue.text: Choose a musical number at start, or end, of Turandot

parts.note: op. (opus) is the abbreviation for a numbered musical work

indicators.note: Turandot both begins and ends with the same letter, so either end supplies the one needed

explanation.surface: Picking a song from the opening or closing of Puccini's opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Turandot is Puccini's last opera; its first letter and its last are both T.
explanation.definitionFit: To opt is to select or make a choice.

clue.text: A sporting challenge involving most of the Olympic nations for starters?

definitions.text: A sporting challenge involving most of the Olympic nations for starters?

indicators.note: involving means taking something in, so the short piece goes inside the challenge word

parts.note: a trial is a test or challenge

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its final letter
starters are beginnings, so the first letter of each of the two words is used

explanation.surface: A sports event in which nearly every Olympic country competes as an opener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' puts the trimmed 'the' inside the challenge word. The whole clue also describes the event, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A triathlon is a sporting contest of swimming, cycling and running, an Olympic event entered by many nations.

clue.text: December 1873, American author

parts.note: a novelist of the American prairies born in December 1873, marking an anniversary

explanation.surface: A birth date and a profession, like an anniversary listing.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the anniversary clues: the author of My Antonia was born on 7 December 1873.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pulitzer-winning novelist of O Pioneers! was born in Virginia in December 1873.

clue.text: Retain a modicum of liberty perhaps finding Sands's escape route

indicators.note: perhaps suggests one possible version of the letters, signalling a rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

indicators.note: a modicum is a tiny amount, so only the first letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Holding on to a scrap of freedom while finding a way out.
explanation.walkthrough: RETAIN plus L (from 'liberty') is rearranged. Philippe Sands wrote The Ratline, about a Nazi official's flight after the war.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratline is a secret escape route, especially those used by Nazis fleeing Europe, the subject of Philippe Sands's book.

clue.text: January 1873, Jewish poet

parts.note: a Hebrew-language poet born in January 1873, marking an anniversary

explanation.surface: A birth date and a profession, like an anniversary listing.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the anniversary clues: Hayim Nahman, Israel's national poet, was born in January 1873.
explanation.definitionFit: Hayim Nahman of that surname, a pioneer of modern Hebrew poetry, was born in Ukraine in January 1873.

clue.text: Confusing T. S. Eliot recipe for verses

indicators.note: confusing means mixing up, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the poet's initials and surname taken as written
R is the abbreviation for recipe, as in Rx on prescriptions

explanation.surface: Muddling the poet's instructions for writing poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: TSELIOT plus R is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Triolets are short fixed-form poems of eight lines with repeated refrains, so they are verses.

clue.text: Pet in Orwell's days, about start of twenties

parts.note: Burmese Days is George Orwell's first novel
ca. (circa) means about

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An animal kept by Orwell during his time abroad, around the 1920s.
explanation.walkthrough: Orwell served in the police in Burma in the 1920s, which makes the surface plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: This breed of domestic cat is a common household animal kept for companionship.

clue.text: Type of dramatic performance I really camp up

indicators.note: up here means stirred up or in disorder, signalling a rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An actor confesses to hamming it up on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A miracle play is a medieval drama presenting saints' lives, a form of theatrical performance.

clue.text: Balancé represented by French painter (b. 1823)

indicators.note: represented means presented again in another form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: a ballet step, taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A ballet step depicted by a nineteenth-century French artist.
explanation.walkthrough: A balancé is a rocking dance step; its letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandre Cabanel, born in Montpellier in 1823, was an academic painter of the French Second Empire.

clue.text: Forster character unaltered in hearing

indicators.note: signals that the phrase for unaltered is taken by its sound when spoken

parts.note: unaltered means as is, left the way it was

explanation.surface: A novelist's character remains unchanged at a court hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Aziz is the Indian doctor at the centre of E. M. Forster's novel A Passage to India.

clue.text: "Metre in verse", as an example

parts.note: the quoted phrase, stressed on its first and last syllables with two light ones between, is itself a specimen of a particular metrical foot

explanation.surface: A phrase offered as an example of poetic rhythm.
explanation.walkthrough: Say it: ME-tre in VERSE, long-short-short-long, the four-syllable foot named here.
explanation.definitionFit: A choriamb is a metrical foot of one stressed syllable, two unstressed and a stressed one, the pattern the quoted phrase follows.

clue.text: June 1723, Scottish economist

parts.note: the author of The Wealth of Nations, born in June 1723, marking an anniversary

explanation.surface: A birth date and a profession, like an anniversary listing.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the anniversary clues: the Kirkcaldy-born economist was baptised on 5 June 1723.
explanation.definitionFit: The father of modern economics, who wrote The Wealth of Nations, was born in Kirkcaldy in June 1723.

clue.text: Anthropologist in East Africa with set of answers to the origin of life

indicators.note: the origin of a word is where it begins, its first letter

parts.note: EA is the abbreviation for East Africa
a key is a set of answers, as at the back of a textbook

explanation.surface: A scientist in Kenya holding the answers to how life began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' sets the region and the answer key after the first letter of 'life'. Louis and Mary Leakey searched East Africa for human origins, so the surface fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Leakey was a Kenyan-born scientist who studied early human fossils, the work of a palaeoanthropologist.

clue.text: Mistress of Commodus, top-class stuff on reflection

indicators.note: reflection reverses an image, so the combined letters are read backwards

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, written here with the letter I for the figure one
to cram is to stuff

explanation.surface: An emperor's lover is really first-rate material, when you think about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on reflection' turns AICRAM round. A1 is entered as AI, the usual crossword liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcia was the concubine of the Roman emperor Commodus who helped plot his murder.

clue.text: In the morning grandmaster Larsen enthrals one and all around

parts.note: AM (ante meridiem) means in the morning

indicators.note: enthrals means holds captive, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: Bent Larsen was a Danish chess grandmaster
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A chess master captivates everyone at a morning game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enthrals' puts the numeral inside the Danish player's first name, making BIENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambient describes the surrounding conditions, the environment on every side.

clue.text: "So munch on, crunch on, take your r —— " ("The Pied Piper of Hamelin")

definitions.text: "So munch on, crunch on, take your r —— " ("The Pied Piper of Hamelin")

parts.words: "So munch on, crunch on, take your r —— " ("The Pied Piper of Hamelin")
parts.note: a line from Browning's poem, where the rats are promised a feast; the missing word is an old term for a light midday snack, rhyming with munch on and crunch on

explanation.surface: A quotation from Browning with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'r' ends 'your' and the missing word follows, completing the rhyme on 'crunch on'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuncheon is an archaic word for a light snack between meals, which the Piper's music promises the rats.

clue.text: Places to buy Stout's novel involving the essence of puzzlement

indicators.note: involving means taking in, so one piece goes inside the other
novel means new or fresh, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

parts.note: the name taken as written, the possessive adding no letter

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, its two middle letters

explanation.surface: Bookshops stock a detective novel by Rex Stout with a puzzling plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' rearranges the author's name to OUTTS, and 'involving' puts the core of 'puzzlement' inside. Rex Stout wrote the Nero Wolfe mysteries.
explanation.definitionFit: Outlets are shops or stores where goods are sold.

clue.text: September 1923, Welsh poet

parts.note: a Cardiff-born poet and physician born in September 1923, marking an anniversary

explanation.surface: A birth date and a profession, like an anniversary listing.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the anniversary clues: Dannie, poet and doctor, was born in Cardiff on 22 September 1923.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh poet Dannie of that surname, also a chest physician, was born in September 1923.

clue.text: Is idolatry at variance with unanimity?

indicators.note: at variance means differing, so the letters are put into a different order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A philosophical question about whether worship of idols conflicts with agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: Solidarity is unity of feeling or purpose among a group, a shared agreement.

clue.text: Duke with some land, Trevor-Roper for one

parts.note: an acre is a measured area of land

explanation.surface: A nobleman with an estate, like a historian peer.
explanation.walkthrough: The historian Hugh Trevor-Roper became Lord Dacre of Glanton, hence 'for one'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Trevor-Roper was made a life peer as Baron Dacre, one holder of that title.

clue.text: French writer penning one of his articles on current French poet

indicators.note: penning means enclosing as in a pen, so the other letters go inside

parts.note: Jules Verne was the French author of science fiction
la is a French definite article, his language being French
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A novelist writes an essay about a contemporary poet.
explanation.walkthrough: LA and I go inside VERNE. 'current' looks like 'contemporary' but is the physics symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Verlaine was a nineteenth-century Symbolist poet from France.

clue.text: Cash realized by Owen Wilson in The Royal Tenenbaums

definitions.text: Cash realized by Owen Wilson in The Royal Tenenbaums

parts.words: Cash realized by Owen Wilson in The Royal Tenenbaums
parts.note: Cash is a surname, not money: Owen Wilson played a character so surnamed in the Wes Anderson film, and the first name is wanted

explanation.surface: Money made by an actor from a Wes Anderson film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cash' and 'realized' suggest money earned; Cash is the character's surname and 'realized' means portrayed.
explanation.definitionFit: Owen Wilson's role in The Royal Tenenbaums is the novelist with this first name and the surname Cash.

clue.text: December 1773, the father of aviation

parts.note: a Yorkshire engineer born in December 1773 who designed early gliders, marking an anniversary

explanation.surface: A birth date and a title, like an anniversary listing.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the anniversary clues: Sir George, the glider pioneer, was born on 27 December 1773.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir George of that surname, who set out the principles of heavier-than-air flight, was born in December 1773.

clue.text: Scott's astrologer, a chap returning for a long spell in India

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the word is read in reverse up this down light

parts.note: Guy Mannering is the astrologer hero of Walter Scott's novel, and a guy is a chap

explanation.surface: A fortune-teller from a novel goes back to India for a long stay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns GUY round.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hindu cosmology a yug or yuga is one of the great ages of the world, a vast period of time.

clue.text: "— is a grand tonic, Kemp, to take the flabbiness out of a man" (The Invisible Man)

definitions.text: "— is a grand tonic, Kemp, to take the flabbiness out of a man" (The Invisible Man)

parts.words: "— is a grand tonic, Kemp, to take the flabbiness out of a man" (The Invisible Man)
parts.note: a line from H. G. Wells's novel in which Griffin praises a bitter poison, once used in small doses as a stimulant

explanation.surface: A quotation from H. G. Wells with its first word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Strychnine, a deadly alkaloid poison, was once taken in tiny doses as a tonic, as Griffin says to Kemp.

clue.text: Lead parts in Grand Hotel include one singular Hollywood actress

indicators.note: include means take in, so the other letters go between
the lead parts of words are their first letters

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular

explanation.surface: The starring roles in a classic film go to a solo screen star.
explanation.walkthrough: IS goes between G and H. Grand Hotel is a 1932 MGM film, making the surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Lillian Gish was a silent-film star of the American screen.
